title: Two Sisters, Two Certainties
script: Mira: [pointed] You do realize Mother still introduces you as 'my daughter, the doctoral candidate,' and me as simply 'my other daughter,' as though carpentry doesn't merit a noun.
Sinta: [amused] She'll come around. Give her another decade and a properly finished dining table.
Mira: [wry] I don't doubt your competence, Sinta. I doubt my own, increasingly, which is a considerably less charming thing to say out loud at family dinners.
Sinta: [curious] What's actually prompting this? You've never once envied the workshop before.
Mira: [candid] Six years into this degree, I've started wondering whether I chose depth or simply chose delay, postponing the terror of an ordinary life by disguising it as intellectual ambition.
Sinta: [gentle] That's a harsh verdict to pass on yourself over one difficult semester.
Mira: [honest] Maybe. But you built something tangible by twenty-four. I have footnotes, and a persistent suspicion that footnotes don't actually keep anyone warm.
Sinta: [thoughtful] They don't, no. But neither does a table, not literally. What kept our childhood warm wasn't furniture, it was Mother's insistence that curiosity mattered as much as usefulness.
Mira: [surprised] I hadn't expected the philosophy student to end up in the workshop and the carpenter to end up defending philosophy.
Sinta: [smiling] Somebody had to keep the argument alive between us. You were too busy footnoting it into submission.
Mira: [wry] Fair. Though I still maintain a dining table is a more legible achievement than a chapter nobody outside three specialists will ever read.
Sinta: [firm] Legible to whom, though? I can't explain load-bearing joints to Mother's book club, and I doubt they'd applaud if I tried.
Mira: [conceding] Point taken. Perhaps we've both just chosen forms of mastery illegible to the people not already fluent in them.
Sinta: [warmly] Now you're finally sounding like the philosopher again, instead of someone auditioning for my job out of spite.

quiz.question: How does the sisters' mother introduce Sinta, according to Mira?
options: As 'my daughter, the doctoral candidate'
As 'my other daughter,' without further description
As 'my brilliant carpenter'
She never mentions Sinta
quiz.explanation: Mira points out their mother introduces Sinta simply as 'my other daughter,' unlike Mira's title.

quiz.question: What does Mira begin to suspect about her six years pursuing the doctoral degree?
options: That it was clearly the right choice
That she may have chosen delay disguised as intellectual ambition rather than depth
That her sister forced her into it
That the degree was too easy
quiz.explanation: Mira wonders whether she chose depth or simply delay, disguising terror of ordinary life as intellectual ambition.

quiz.question: What does Sinta say kept their childhood warm, beyond furniture?
options: Wealth and status
Their mother's insistence that curiosity mattered as much as usefulness
Strict discipline
Nothing in particular
quiz.explanation: Sinta says what kept their childhood warm was their mother's insistence that curiosity mattered as much as usefulness.

quiz.question: What surprises Mira about how the conversation has unfolded?
options: That Sinta agrees with everything she says
That the philosophy student ended up in the workshop and the carpenter ended up defending philosophy
That their mother joined the conversation
That Sinta wants to quit carpentry
quiz.explanation: Mira is surprised the philosophy-inclined sister became the carpenter while the carpenter defends philosophy.

quiz.question: What conclusion do the sisters reach about their respective paths?
options: One path is clearly superior
They have both chosen forms of mastery illegible to people not already fluent in them
Neither path has any value
They should switch careers
quiz.explanation: Mira concludes they've both chosen forms of mastery illegible to those not already fluent in them.
